package.title: GLP-1 vs CPAP for Sleep Apnea: What the Numbers Show

social.instagram_caption:
Can a GLP-1 shot replace your CPAP mask? 😮

Here's what the actual trial data shows:

→ SURMOUNT-OSA: adults with obesity + moderate-to-severe sleep apnea lost about 18–20% of body weight on tirzepatide over 52 weeks
→ Their breathing pauses (AHI) dropped roughly 51–59% on average, vs only ~3% on placebo
→ Dec 2024: tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved medicine for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity
→ But in a rough comparison across different trials, CPAP still cut more events per hour on average. It's not an either/or

The takeaway: a GLP-1 can meaningfully ease sleep apnea severity by helping the airway, but it isn't a proven substitute for CPAP. Keep using CPAP unless your sleep clinician changes your plan, and ask whether adding a GLP-1 fits your plan. It's a prescription medicine, so talk to your doctor about whether it's right for you.

Save this for your next sleep appointment, and send it to your CPAP buddy 💙

Have you talked to your doctor about GLP-1s and sleep apnea? Tell us below 👇

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation.

social.facebook_caption:
Can a GLP-1 medicine replace your CPAP machine? The short answer: no — but it can be a helpful teammate. Keep using CPAP unless your sleep clinician changes your plan.

In the SURMOUNT-OSA trial, adults with obesity and moderate-to-severe sleep apnea who took tirzepatide saw their breathing pauses drop by about 51–59% on average over a year, compared to about 3% on placebo. That's a big deal — enough that in December 2024, the FDA approved tirzepatide as the first medicine for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

But in a rough comparison across different trials, CPAP still cut more breathing pauses per hour on average. The two work differently: CPAP holds your airway open with air pressure whenever it's worn, while weight loss from a GLP-1 gradually eases pressure on the airway over months. Tirzepatide also lowered breathing pauses in people who already use CPAP, so ask your sleep doctor whether using both fits your plan.

If you use CPAP or have sleep apnea, would you ask your doctor about adding a GLP-1 to your plan? It's a prescription medicine, so talk to your doctor about whether it's right for you. carousel.title: GLP-1 vs CPAP for Sleep Apnea: What the Numbers Show

slides.headline: Can a GLP-1 replace your CPAP?
slides.bubble: Wait… could a weekly shot beat my mask?!

slides.headline: Where moderate sleep apnea starts on AHI
slides.body: AHI counts full or partial breathing pauses per hour of sleep, measured in a sleep study. The SURMOUNT-OSA trial enrolled adults with 15 or more (moderate-to-severe).

slides.headline: Why weight loss can help the airway
slides.body: In SURMOUNT-OSA, weight fell about 18–20% on tirzepatide vs about 2% on placebo over 52 weeks.

items.label: Extra weight near airway
items.detail: Fat deposits can narrow the upper airway

items.label: Airway sags in sleep
items.detail: Relaxed muscles plus tight space mean pauses

items.label: GLP-1 medicine quiets appetite
items.detail: Tirzepatide (GIP/GLP-1): lowers appetite and food intake, so weight comes down gradually

items.label: More room to breathe
items.detail: Fewer pauses per hour for many people

slides.headline: Breathing pauses cut per hour after 1 year
slides.body: Average drop in AHI events per hour after 52 weeks, SURMOUNT-OSA (NEJM 2024): two trials in adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and obesity. Relative drop: about 51–59% on tirzepatide vs about 3% on placebo.
slides.bubble: Plot twist: it helped people who already use CPAP too!

slides.headline: First medicine FDA-approved for obstructive sleep apnea
slides.body: Dec 2024: the FDA approved tirzepatide (Zepbound) for moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity (FDA).

slides.headline: Myth: on a GLP-1, you can ditch CPAP
slides.body: Fact: in SURMOUNT-OSA, tirzepatide roughly halved breathing pauses on average. It didn't erase them. Keep using CPAP unless your sleep clinician changes your plan.

slides.headline: Questions to bring to your sleep doctor
slides.body: It's a prescription medicine and isn't right for everyone (e.g. during pregnancy or with certain thyroid or pancreas history). Your clinician can tell you whether it's right for you.

items.label: Could a GLP-1 fit my plan?
items.detail: Ask if you meet the approval criteria

items.label: Should I keep my CPAP?
items.detail: Don't change it without your clinician

items.label: When should I retest?
items.detail: Ask about a repeat sleep study

items.label: Which side effects are common?
items.detail: Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation are common, mostly early on

slides.headline: CPAP still cuts more pauses per hour
slides.body: Drop in events per hour compared with placebo or usual care, pooled from meta-analyses (JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery review, 2026). Tirzepatide cut about 20–24 more than placebo, at the top of the GLP-1 range. Different trials, so this is a rough comparison.

slides.headline: Save this for your next sleep appointment
slides.body: In adults with obesity, a GLP-1 medicine can cut sleep apnea severity, and CPAP still does the heavy lifting. Ask your sleep doctor whether using both fits your plan.

factcheck.summary:
The carousel is accurate and safe to publish. I checked every number against a source:
- **AHI drops (SURMOUNT-OSA, treatment-regimen estimand):** tirzepatide −25.3/h vs placebo −5.3/h in people not on CPAP, and −29.3/h vs −5.5/h in CPAP users.
- **Relative drops:** −50.7% and −58.7% on tirzepatide vs −3.0% and −2.5% on placebo.
- **Weight change:** −17.7% and −19.6% on tirzepatide vs −1.6% and −2.3% on placebo.
- **FDA approval:** 20 Dec 2024, adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and obesity, alongside diet and exercise.
- **JAMA Oto review (2026):** confirmed to exist (Harris & Kaffenberger, doi:10.1001/jamaoto.2026.2266, online 3 Sep 2026). It gives GLP-1 RA meta-analysis ranges of −5.7 to −21.9 events/h, tirzepatide at 20–24 below placebo, and CPAP at about 31 vs about 22.

The safety framing is good: "keep using CPAP unless your clinician changes your plan", plus thyroid, pancreas and pregnancy caveats and a list of common side effects. Two minor wording fixes are listed below. They're optional polish and don't block publishing. The NEJM page returns 403 to automated fetching, but the article exists, and its figures match Lilly's release of the trial data.

issues.claim: GLP-1 medicines: events cut per hour 'About 6–22'; CPAP 'About 31'; 'Tirzepatide was at the top of the GLP-1 range.'
issues.problem: Slide 4 shows tirzepatide's raw drops of 25.3 and 29.3/h. Slide 8's GLP-1 range is placebo-comparison meta-analysis figures, and tirzepatide's difference from placebo (20–24/h) actually goes a bit above 22. Without a note, viewers may see 29.3 vs 31 and think the numbers disagree.
issues.fix: Replace the Slide 8 body with: "Drop in events per hour compared with placebo or usual care, pooled from meta-analyses (JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery review, 2026). Tirzepatide cut about 20–24 more than placebo, at the top of the GLP-1 range. Different trials, so this is a rough comparison."

issues.claim: Tirzepatide (GIP/GLP-1): less food noise, gradual weight loss
issues.problem: SURMOUNT-OSA didn't measure 'food noise'. The FDA describes the mechanism as reducing appetite and food intake.
issues.fix: Tirzepatide (GIP/GLP-1): lowers appetite and food intake, so weight comes down gradually
